# Part 1 - Navigating and Managing Files

1.  Downloading *The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes* from Project Gutenberg:

``` bash
curl -o "holmes.txt" https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/1661/pg1661.txt
```

2.  Confirm the file downloaded and its size:

``` bash
ls -l
```

3.  Creating nestled folders:

``` bash
mkdir -p drafts/working/final
```

4.  Creating empty file:

``` bash
touch log.txt
```

5.  Moving the empty file to folder:

``` bash
mv log.txt drafts/working/final/
```

6.  Renaming the folder:

``` bash
mv drafts/ notes/
```

7.  Creating throwaway folder and removing it:

``` bash
mkdir scratch
rm -r scratch/
```

8.  Writing a script and running it

``` bash
touch setup.sh
```

- The script:

  ``` bash
  mkdir backup_check
  cd backup_check
  curl -o holmes.txt https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/1661/pg1661.txt
  echo "Downloaded holmes.txt"
  ```

- Running it:

  ``` bash
  source setup.sh
  ```

- Confirming it worked:

  ``` bash
  ls
  ```

**Answer:** Both rmdir and rm -r are used to delete empty folders, but rmdir only works on completely empty folders while rm -r removes the folder and everything inside it without any safeguards, so it's more dangerous. Either command would have worked for step 7 since the scratch folder was completely empty.

# Part 2 - Counting and Searching

9.  Using wc, wc -l, and wc -w:

``` bash
bash wc holmes.txt
```

12310 107558 607606 holmes.txt

``` bash
wc -l holmes.txt
```

12310 holmes.txt

``` bash
wc -w holmes.txt
```

107558 holmes.txt

10. Searching for the word "Watson" in the text:

``` bash
grep "Watson" holmes.txt
```

- Piping:
``` bash
grep "Watson" holmes.txt | wc -l
```

11. Searching for the word "Holmes" in the text:
``` bash
grep "Holmes" holmes.txt | wc -l
``` 

- Holmes appears in 460 lines of the text while Watson appears in 81 lines of the text.

# Part 4 - Reflection
The easiest parts of this assignment were the first two parts because I am more familiar with navigating/managing files in the terminal as well as searching for strings with wc, grep, and piping. The most difficult part of this assignment was the last two parts because I had to use regular expressions to search for patterns in the text. I had to look up some of the commands for regular expressions and test them out in the terminal to make sure they worked correctly. I got to be more familiar with VSCode and creating this assignment with its built-in editors. With this knowledge, I can use these commands to research and analyze the repetition or percentage of words with three or more consecutive vowels in large text files.
